Brown” as school inspector (f1839_r0041, printed page 38). What a match may carry, and it depends on WHICH TABLE it landed in. A match on the sheriffs' rows of 1831, 1832, 1834 or 1836 is different in kind: the office is contemporary with the town, the 1834 row's term covers the scene date outright, and such a match carries reaches_scene. Even there the SOURCE is a retrospect — a table running to 1874, set in 1876 out of Old Settlers' recollections per the compiler's warning on printed page 3 — so it may be cited as a contemporary office and may not be graded `documented` without a second, nearer record. The ward on printed page 38 is a ward of the CITY of 1839 and places no house in the town of 1835. (data/research/directories/fergus_1839_election_crosswalk_1835.json and fergus_1839_register_crosswalk_1835.json). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a poll twenty-two months after the scene date — or a register four years after it — is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE rather than about July 1835. T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict. THE FEDERAL LAND TRACT SALES — A PURCHASE, AND NEVER A RESIDENCE. (data/research/land_sales/resident_crosswalk.json). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. This project has ruled the head a CANDIDATE and no more: the name agrees and is unique on both sides, but the reader graded the name on the sheet low, and a low-confidence read caps at a candidate however well the name agrees. THE SECOND PRESBYTERIAN ROLL — A NAME ON A CHURCH LIST THAT OPENS IN 1842, AND NEVER AN 1835 FACT. The 1892 printed membership roll of the Second Presbyterian Church of Chicago, read line by line into this repository, carries 1 line whose surname and given initial agree with this person's — “Brown, William H. | Letter. | June 1, 1842. | Deceased,” (second_presb_0467, printed page 180), admitted 1842-06-01 by letter. persons.name: John Wright
persons.note: ONE OF THE TWELVE WHO VOTED FOR INCORPORATION on 5 August 1833 (Andreas prints the poll: 'John W. Wright'), one of the twenty-eight electors five days later, a candidate who took two votes, and one of the nine village citizens founding the First Presbyterian Church on 26 June 1833 and one of its three first elders. Charles Butler met him on his first morning in Chicago in August 1833, at the funeral of a child. The Chicago Democrat of 26 November 1833 is the only contemporary Chicago document this project holds, and an advertisement in it is a peculiarly good witness: the advertiser was paying for it and his customers had to be able to find him. It is also NINETEEN MONTHS before the scene date, in the town's fastest-changing period, so it is strong evidence of existence and address in November 1833 and weak evidence of survival to 1 July 1835.

persons.name: John S. Wright
persons.note: A MINOR IN 1833 AND A FOUNDING MEMBER OF THE FIRST PRESBYTERIAN CHURCH IN JUNE OF THAT YEAR - his name is in the list of nine village citizens alongside his father's. He would have been about twenty in 1835. THE RELATIONSHIP IS THIS RECORD'S READING: Andreas lists the two Wrights separately and never says they are father and son, and 'John Wright, came in 1832, a merchant' and 'John S. Wright, then a minor ... came in 1832' arriving in the same year with the same surname and joining the same church on the same day is a strong reading and not a statement.

research_note: RECONSTRUCTED / GENERATED, NOT AN ATTESTED NAMED BUILDING. The block, its scheduled roof count and its family mix follow the 665-roof programme; exact presence, lot, position, footprint, finish and instance-level form are interpretive. H-family house massing currently resolves through the frame dwelling archetype; no larger house generator is implemented. TWO OF THIS FAMILY'S NAMED VARIANTS ARE REFUSED AND TWO STAND (T-1686): the hip its roof line offers ("side gable or hip, 6:12-9:12") is refused rather than quietly substituted, because a hip, gambrel or mansard roof on a Chicago house in 1835 would be a claim and not a default; the Greek doorway its variants name is refused BY DATE — the earliest Greek Revival house in Chicago is the Clarke House of 1836, which data/exclusions.json keeps out of this scene, so no entablature, corner pilaster or portico stands on a roof of 1835-07-01; and the corner boards and the one-to-two chimneys the same line names already stand: the trim follows the stud module the construction argument picks.
